spike: SPIKE 8 — does a real MCP client tolerate a stateless server (no Mcp-Session-Id, 405 on GET, 405 on DELETE)?
claim: An MCP client built on @modelcontextprotocol/sdk tolerates a server that (a) never issues `Mcp-Session-Id`, (b) answers `405` to GET on the MCP endpoint, and (c) answers `405` to DELETE — a full initialize → tools/list → tools/call → close cycle succeeds with no error, warning, or stderr output.
what_i_ran: `node spike-8-stateless-client-tolerance.mjs` (main), `node spike-8b-delete-405-and-reuse.mjs`, `node spike-8c-reuse-detail.mjs` — all in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-nguyenhanh-orca-projects-MCPRouter/4911361f-32f3-47c8-97c7-182f1fc87bd2/scratchpad/spikes/. The main script stands up a node:http `/mcp` that logs every method+headers, returns `405 Allow: POST` for GET and DELETE, strips `Mcp-Session-Id` from every response via a `setHeader`/`writeHead` monkeypatch, and serves POST from a fresh McpServer + StreamableHTTPServerTransport({sessionIdGenerator: undefined}); then drives it with a real SDK `Client` + `StreamableHTTPClientTransport`.

impact: Spec §14 assumption 8 stands as written for SDK-based clients: no fallback needed, no session store, no GET/SSE endpoint, no DELETE handler beyond a flat 405. BUT the spec must add one constraint it does not currently state: **the stateless server transport is single-use.** `webStandardStreamableHttp.js:172-176` throws on the second `handleRequest` of the same instance, and the failure is not theoretical — it kills even a single client's handshake, because the `notifications/initialized` POST is already request #2 (spike-8c: POST 1 → 200, POST 2 → 500). The gateway's `/mcp` handler must construct a fresh `McpServer` + `StreamableHTTPServerTransport` inside the request, register tools there, and tear both down on `res` close. That reshapes the handler (and makes tool-registration cost per-request, which matters if the tool list is built from a remote upstream — cache the descriptors, not the server object). ~15 LOC, but it is a structural constraint, not a detail.
fallback_verified: n/a — claim confirmed, no fallback needed. I did additionally verify the one path the happy case skips: with a session id artificially present (`_sessionId = 'pretend-session-abc'`), `terminateSession()` against a 405 DELETE returns without throwing and clears the id (spike-8b part A). So even a client that somehow holds a session id is not broken by the 405.
gotchas: STATELESS TRANSPORT IS SINGLE-USE. `new StreamableHTTPServerTransport({sessionIdGenerator: undefined})` throws 'Stateless transport cannot be reused across requests' on its 2nd handleRequest (webStandardStreamableHttp.js:174). It surfaces to the client as an opaque `Streamable HTTP error: Error POSTing to endpoint:` with an EMPTY body and a 500 — nothing in the message hints at reuse. Build the server+transport inside the request handler.

The client DOES issue a GET, but only after the `notifications/initialized` POST returns 202 — so a gateway that answers initialized with 200+body instead of 202 will never see the GET at all. Either way the 405 is swallowed at client/streamableHttp.js:103 with no onerror and nothing on stderr.

`client.close()` NEVER sends DELETE (client/streamableHttp.js:281-288 just aborts). The DELETE only happens if app code calls `transport.terminateSession()` explicitly — and that is a no-op when no session id was ever issued. So in stateless mode the DELETE-405 branch is, in practice, dead code for the SDK client. It is still worth returning 405 rather than 404/500 for clients that do call it.

Negotiated protocol version was `2025-11-25` (the SDK's LATEST), and from the 2nd request onward the client sends `mcp-protocol-version: 2025-11-25` on every request — including the GET. If the gateway validates or routes on headers, that is the header it will see, not `mcp-session-id`.

The SDK server answers a single JSON-RPC request with `content-type: text/event-stream` (a one-event SSE body) by default, not `application/json`. Pass `enableJsonResponse: true` if any proxy/CDN in front of the gateway mishandles SSE.

Unsupported methods handled by the SDK itself return `Allow: GET, POST, DELETE` (webStandardStreamableHttp.js:441-455) — if the gateway wants to advertise `Allow: POST` it must intercept GET/DELETE before handing the request to the transport, as the spike does.
